title: Data skills for a public-health service team — example course

provider.name: Example training provider (demonstration)
provider.assessmentRequirements: Complete the three practical tasks and the independent question set. Submit your interpretation, relevant report/R output and a reflection for tutor review. This demonstration is not an accredited course.
provider.cpdStatement: No CPD credit is attached to this example. A real provider must specify its own recognised scheme and assessment conditions.

documents.title: Example provider notes: interpreting service data
documents.text: Start with a defined population, outcome and time period. Check how the observations were collected. Repeated measurements on the same people are paired; different people measured in two periods are not automatically paired. A change after training is an association in a before-and-after study. Without a suitable comparison, other changes, selection or regression to the mean can explain it. Report the size and uncertainty of a change and its practical implications, not only a P value.

lessons.title: Define a useful service question
lessons.objective: Define an outcome, target population, unit of observation and comparison before choosing an analysis.
lessons.summary: A public-health team wants to reduce the time needed to prepare a weekly service report. The same eight staff members time one comparable report before and one after training. These are fictional data.
lessons.steps: Identify the measured unit and why the observations form pairs. Consider whether one report per staff member represents routine performance.
lessons.challenge: Specify the population, outcome, units and comparison. Give one limitation of using these eight staff members to generalise to other teams.

lessons.title: From a worksheet to a paired analysis
lessons.objective: Analyse within-person differences and explain the estimated change and confidence interval.
lessons.summary: Each row represents the same staff member before and after training. Times are minutes per report. Positive before-minus-after differences represent shorter report preparation after training.
lessons.steps: Choose Try in StatsDirect and run the paired t test. Inspect the differences, consider the assumptions, and report the mean reduction with its confidence interval. Eight pairs provide limited information about the distribution of differences.
lessons.challenge: Record the estimated mean reduction and 95% confidence interval. Explain the meaning of pairing and one reason to be cautious about interpretation.
lessons.r:
before <- c(12,11,15,14,10,13,16,12)
after <- c(10,10,11,13,9,10,14,10)
data <- data.frame(before, after)
print(data)
print(t.test(data$before, data$after, paired=TRUE, conf.level=0.95))
plot(data$before-data$after, ylab="Reduction in minutes", xlab="Staff member")
abline(h=0, lty=2)

lessons.title: Separate improvement from a causal claim
lessons.objective: Distinguish an observed change from evidence that training caused it.
lessons.summary: A before-and-after comparison can show a change within staff. A paired t test alone does not establish why it occurred. Changes in report complexity, software or workload could also matter.
lessons.steps: Consider a concurrent comparison group, consistent outcome measurement and a suitable allocation design for a future evaluation. Explain the implications in language a service manager can use.
lessons.challenge: Write a short recommendation to the manager, including uncertainty, one alternative explanation and a stronger design for evaluating the training. Add a reflection on how this changes your usual use of Excel.

questions.stem: Which analysis directly uses the matching in the report-preparation example?

options.text: A paired analysis of each staff member’s before-minus-after difference
An unpaired analysis treating the two sets as unrelated
A chi-square test of the two means

questions.explanation: Each staff member is measured twice. The paired analysis uses the within-person difference. Pairing depends on the design, not whether the two columns have the same length.
questions.objective: Interpret a paired service evaluation with appropriate uncertainty and causal caution.

questions.stem: The mean preparation time is lower after training. Which conclusion is justified by this before-and-after study alone?

options.text: Training must have caused the reduction
An observed reduction is compatible with training having an effect, but other explanations remain
A small P value rules out all sources of bias

questions.explanation: The observed change does not by itself identify a causal effect. A statistical test does not remove confounding or other systematic differences between time periods.
questions.objective: Interpret a paired service evaluation with appropriate uncertainty and causal caution.

questions.stem: What should accompany the estimated average reduction when reporting the result?

options.text: Only whether P is less than 0.05
A claim that every staff member will improve by exactly the average
The confidence interval, units, study limitations and practical meaning

questions.explanation: An estimate with its confidence interval communicates magnitude and uncertainty under the analysis assumptions. The mean is not a promise about each individual.
questions.objective: Interpret a paired service evaluation with appropriate uncertainty and causal caution.
